info.text: Four questions on Primer 3: library() against install.packages(), reading a pipeline, %>% against |>, and one thing the browser does that RStudio will not. Unlimited attempts, immediate feedback, zero weight.

questiontext.text:
Four stations were marked out of 100: 16, 25, 36 and 49.

c(16, 25, 36, 49) |> mean() |> sqrt() |> round(2)

What does that print?

generalfeedback.text: 5.61. Read it left to right, in the order the work happens: take these four marks, take the mean (31.5), take the square root (5.6124…), round to two decimal places. The nested version — round(sqrt(mean(c(16, 25, 36, 49))), 2) — gives the same answer but has to be read from the inside out.

feedback.text: That is the mean, which is only the first step. The value then continues along the pipeline into sqrt() and round(2).
That is the answer one step early — round(2) has not been applied. It means two decimal places, so 5.6124… becomes 5.61.

answer.text: An error — you cannot chain three functions in one line

feedback.text: You can, and that is the point of the pipe. Each step hands its result to the next one; a real analysis is often six or seven steps long.

questiontext.text:
In RStudio you run a script that begins with n_distinct(qualifications) and R answers:

Error in n_distinct(qualifications) :
  could not find function "n_distinct"

You installed dplyr last week and it worked then. What is the most likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: You install a package once, ever; you load it every session. Restarting R clears the loaded packages, so a script that worked yesterday fails today unless library(dplyr) is written into the script itself. This is the most common error a beginner meets in R, and its fix is always the same.

answer.text: The script never ran library(dplyr) in this session

feedback.text: Correct. Put library(dplyr) at the top of the script, not just in the console once.

Then library(dplyr) itself would have stopped with a different message — there is no package called 'dplyr'. Reading which of those two messages you got tells you whether to install or to load, so it is worth the ten seconds.
Not R's syntax. You can write dplyr::n_distinct() with two colons to call a function without attaching the package, which is a genuinely useful trick, but the dot form does not exist.
That is a real error, but a different one: it reads object 'qualifications' not found. Here R is complaining about the function, so read the message carefully — it names which of the two is missing.

questiontext.text:
Searching online for help, you find an answer written like this:

students %>% filter(batch == 2024)

What should you make of %>%?

generalfeedback.text: %>% is the magrittr pipe, which predates R's own. For everything in this workshop the two behave the same way, so online answers written with it are still useful to you. We use |> because it is built into R and needs no package — a script using it runs anywhere, with nothing loaded.

answer.text: It is an older pipe that behaves the same way here; you can read the answer and rewrite it with |>

feedback.text: Correct — and you will meet it constantly, because most tutorials online were written before |> existed.

answer.text: It is a typo and the code will not run

feedback.text: No — it is valid R, provided a package such as dplyr or magrittr is loaded to supply it. Dismissing every answer written with %>% would cut you off from most of the R help online.

answer.text: It does something different: it assigns the result back into students

feedback.text: No. That would be %<>%, a rarely used magrittr operator. A plain %>% passes the value along and changes nothing.
No — it comes from a package, not from the editor. It is |> that has the wider reach, because it is part of R itself (from version 4.1) and needs nothing loaded at all.

name.text: P3Q4 What the browser does for you

questiontext.text:
The primer pages load dplyr for you before you run anything, so library(dplyr) is not really needed.

Therefore you can leave library() calls out of the scripts you write in RStudio too.

generalfeedback.text: False, and this is the one way the browser primers actively mislead you. Those pages attach their packages before the first cell runs, so library(dplyr) is a no-op there and essential in RStudio. Type it anyway on the primer page — it is the habit that matters, and a script that forgets it fails with could not find function.

feedback.text: No — this is the trap the primer warns about. The browser page attaches the packages for you; your own RStudio will not. Every script you write needs its library() calls at the top, in every session.
Correct. The browser is the exception, not the rule.
